content.title: About
content.content: White button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus) is one of the most widely cultivated edible fungi worldwide. It has a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a firm yet tender texture. The mushrooms can be eaten raw in salads or cooked by boiling, sautéing, roasting, and more.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White button mushrooms are the young form of the same species that later matures into the brown button (portobello).
In nature, they grow in dense clusters from a single mycelium network.
Vitamin D content increases dramatically after exposure to ultraviolet light.
In Japan, they are a common ingredient in miso soup.
Commercial large‑scale production began in the United States in the 1960s, making them available year‑round.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: 100 g of white button mushrooms provide about 3 g of protein, making them a good meat alternative for vegetarians.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain niacin (B3), riboflavin (B2) and pyridoxine (B6), which support metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and helps maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Very low in fat
items.content: Unlike many nuts and seeds, white button mushrooms contain virtually no fat, fitting well into low‑fat diets.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms, ranging from skin rashes to respiratory issues.

items.title: Mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Improperly stored or damaged mushrooms can develop toxins; always inspect appearance and smell before use.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of raw mushrooms may cause gas and bloating in people with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: White button mushrooms can be eaten raw in salads, pickled, sautéed, stewed, roasted, or added to soups and sauces. Before cooking, gently brush or trim the stems and, if desired, remove the thin skin.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store mushrooms in a paper bag in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C; they stay fresh for 3–5 days. Avoid airtight plastic containers, which accelerate spoilage. Discard any mushrooms that become slimy or develop an off‑odor.
